overview.intro:
Chapter 89 covers every kind of vessel: cruise ships, ferries, tankers and cargo ships (8901), fishing vessels (8902), yachts, motorboats, sailboats, inflatable boats, canoes and kayaks (8903), tugs (8904), dredgers, floating cranes, floating docks and drilling or production platforms (8905), warships, lifeboats and hulls (8906), rafts, buoys and other floating structures (8907) and vessels for scrapping (8908). The U.S. imported **$3.06B** of them in 2025, and **82% were pleasure boats** (heading 8903).

Base rates are low. Every ship, tug, platform and floating structure is **Free**; pleasure boats pay **1% to 2.7%** (canoes and kayaks Free), and most FTA partners pay nothing. The extra duties are what matter. Boats from the **60 Section 301 economies** pay 10% or 12.5% on top (for the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan the total is 10% or 12.5% in place of the base rate), unless Canadian or Mexican goods qualify for USMCA. **China** pays 25% under List 1, 2 or 3 (7.5% for warships and buoys under List 4A) plus 12.5%, **Brazil** 25% plus 12.5%, and **Canadian motorboats, outboard boats, floating docks, hulls, buoys and tanks** pay a **50% Section 338 duty** even with a USMCA claim.

Two maritime rules sit outside the rate table. U.S.-flag ships repaired abroad owe **50% of the foreign repair cost** (19 U.S.C. 1466, heading 9818.00.07), and a foreign-built vessel can never carry cargo or passengers between U.S. ports (the **Jones Act**, 46 U.S.C. 55102). USTR's **port fees on Chinese-operated and Chinese-built ships** are a charge on vessel calls, not an import duty, and are suspended until November 9, 2026. No Section 232 or antidumping duty covers Chapter 89 goods.

productGroups.label: Cruise ships, excursion boats, ferry boats, cargo ships, barges and similar vessels for the transport of persons or goods
productGroups.blurb: Cruise ships, ferries, tankers, refrigerated and cargo ships and barges: 4 lines, all Free (column 2 Free too). U.S. imports are tiny ($2.1M in 2025): ships in international trade enter without a formal entry (additional U.S. note 1), and foreign-built ships cannot carry cargo or passengers between U.S. ports. China pays 37.5% (List 1 or 2 plus 12.5%).

productGroups.label: Fishing vessels; factory ships and other vessels for processing or preserving fishery products
productGroups.blurb: Fishing vessels and factory ships: one line, Free. From the 60 Section 301 economies 10% or 12.5%, from China 37.5% (List 1), from Brazil 37.5%. 2025 imports were $1.3M, mostly from Canada.

productGroups.label: Yachts and other vessels for pleasure or sports; row boats and canoes
productGroups.blurb: Yachts and pleasure boats: inflatable and rigid hull inflatable boats (2.4%), sailboats and motorboats by length (1.5%), outboard motorboats (1%), canoes and kayaks (Free) and other row boats (2.7%). 40 lines, Free under most FTAs. The 2026 Section 301 duty makes most of them 10% to 15.2%; China and Brazil pay 37.5%–40.2%, and Canadian cabin cruisers, motorboats and outboard boats 50% even with USMCA.

productGroups.label: Tugs and pusher craft
productGroups.blurb: Tugs and pusher craft: one line, Free. 10% or 12.5% from the 60 Section 301 economies, 37.5% from China (List 1). $0.3M of imports in 2025.

productGroups.label: Light-vessels, fire-floats, dredgers, floating cranes, and other vessels the navigability of which is subsidiary to their main function; floating docks; floating or submersible drilling or production platforms
productGroups.blurb: Vessels whose navigability is secondary: dredgers, floating or submersible drilling and production platforms (FPSO hulls, semi-submersibles), floating cranes, fire-floats, light-vessels and floating docks. 4 lines, Free (floating docks 35% in column 2). Imports jumped to $407M in 2025, led by $275M of floating platforms from South Korea (12.5%). Canadian floating docks pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Other vessels, including warships and lifeboats other than row boats
productGroups.blurb: Warships and other vessels, including lifeboats and unfinished hulls (chapter note 1 sends a hull without the character of a particular vessel here): 3 lines, Free. China pays 20% on warships (List 4A) and 37.5% on other vessels; Canadian hulls and other vessels pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Other floating structures (for example, rafts, tanks, cofferdams, landing-stages, buoys and beacons)
productGroups.blurb: Floating structures: inflatable life rafts, buoys, floating tanks, cofferdams, landing stages and pontoons. 4 lines, Free (45% in column 2). China pays 37.5% on rafts and 20% on buoys and tanks (List 4A); Canadian buoys and other floating structures pay 50% under Section 338.

productGroups.label: Vessels and other floating structures for breaking up (scrapping)
productGroups.blurb: Vessels and floating structures for breaking up (scrapping): one line, Free. China pays 37.5% (List 1). $35K of imports in 2025.

workedExamples.title: $1M motor yacht from Italy
workedExamples.body: A cabin cruiser over 24 m pays a **1.5%** base rate. Italy is an EU member, so the 2026 Section 301 heading 9903.05.39 sets the total at **10%** whenever the base rate is below 10% (U.S. note 52(k)): **$100,000**. No Chapter 89 line is on the note 52(b) exemption list. From April 5, 2025 to February 23, 2026 it paid the IEEPA reciprocal tariff instead (15% all-inclusive for the EU from August 7, 2025).

workedExamples.title: $250,000 motorboat from Mexico
workedExamples.body: A 7.5–24 m cabin cruiser pays **1.5%**, Free with a USMCA claim (SPI S). The 10% Section 301 duty on Mexico (9903.05.55) does not apply to USMCA goods (note 52(h), 9903.05.94), so the duty is **$0**. Without a USMCA claim it is 1.5% + 10% = **11.5%**: $28,750. Mexico was the largest supplier of pleasure boats in 2025 ($497M).

workedExamples.title: $250,000 cabin cruiser from Canada
workedExamples.body: Since September 15, 2026, Canadian motorboats of 8903.31, 8903.32 and 8903.93.20 are on the Section 338 list in U.S. note 51(b)(1) (9903.03.12, Proclamation 11064). Note 51(a) charges the **50%** even when USMCA is claimed: **$125,000** with a USMCA claim. Without one, the 1.5% base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.29) are added: **61.5%**, $153,750. Canadian sailboats and inflatable boats are not on the list (Free with USMCA).

workedExamples.title: $40,000 fiberglass outboard boat from China
workedExamples.body: An outboard motorboat of reinforced plastics, 5 m or shorter, pays **1%**, plus **25%** under List 3 (9903.88.03) and **12.5%** under the 2026 Section 301 action on China (9903.05.31): **38.5%**, $15,400. No product exclusion for Chapter 89 is in effect (the 2019–2020 exclusions for kayaks, canoes and inflatable boats have expired). The 2025 IEEPA duties on China ended February 24, 2026.

workedExamples.title: $100M floating production platform from South Korea
workedExamples.body: Floating or submersible drilling and production platforms are **Free**. Korea is one of the partners (with the EU, Japan, Switzerland and Taiwan) whose 2026 Section 301 heading (9903.05.71) sets a floor: goods with a base rate below 12.5% pay **12.5%** in total, so the duty is **$12.5M**. The KORUS FTA rate (Free) does not lower it. In 2025 Korea shipped $275M of 8905 goods, the largest single flow outside pleasure boats.

workedExamples.title: $2M of shipyard repairs abroad on a U.S.-flag cargo ship
workedExamples.body: This is not an import of the ship. A vessel documented under U.S. law for foreign or coastwise trade owes **50% of the foreign cost** of equipment and repairs on its first U.S. arrival (19 U.S.C. 1466; heading 9818.00.07, declared on CBP Form 226): **$1M** for repairs in, say, a Chinese yard. Repairs in Canada, Mexico or Israel and FTA partners listed in the special column (for example Korea or Singapore) are free, and crew labor and emergency repairs are excluded (19 CFR 4.14).

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule, the **2025 Basic Edition** (in force January 1, 2025) and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026), and lists every extra duty that reaches Chapter 89 today. **No base rate changed**: all 58 lines carry the same rates.

The extra duties changed a lot. In 2025 non-USMCA boats from Canada and Mexico paid IEEPA duties, boats from almost every other country paid the reciprocal tariff (no Chapter 89 line was on its exemption list), and Brazil paid another 40%. All IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**; the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on **July 23, 2026**.

Today five measures apply: the **2026 Section 301 duties** on 60 economies (from July 24, 2026), **Brazil's 25% Section 301 duty** (from July 22, 2026), **Section 338 at 50%** on Canadian floating docks, hulls, buoys and tanks (from August 22, 2026) and motorboats and outboard boats (from September 15, 2026), China's **Section 301 List 1–4A duties**, and Russia's **35%** in place of column 2. USTR's **maritime Section 301 action** (port fees on Chinese-operated and Chinese-built ships, 100% on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes and chassis) is suspended until November 9, 2026 and never charged a duty on Chapter 89 goods.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 89 from any country: China Section 301 (note 20; the 2024 increases in note 31 list no Chapter 89 line), the 2026 Section 301 actions on 60 economies and Brazil (notes 50, 52), Canada Section 338 (note 51), Russia's rate in lieu of column 2 (note 30), the scheduled Nicaragua Section 301 duty (note 29), and the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties. Also covered for reference: the maritime Section 301 action against China (port fees and crane and chassis duties), the 50% vessel repair duty (Chapter 98 subchapter XVIII) and the Jones Act. No Section 232 action and no antidumping or countervailing duty order covers Chapter 89 goods. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 89 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 58 Chapter 89 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, removed or renumbered. Pleasure boats stay at 1% to 2.7% (canoes and kayaks Free) and every ship, tug, platform and floating structure stays Free.

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China actions, so they did not terminate on their 2026 anniversaries and remain in effect pending the statutory review. The 25% List 1, 2 and 3 duties and the 7.5% List 4A duty on Chinese vessels and boats continue.

changes.title: Section 338: 50% on Canadian motorboats and outboard boats
changes.detail: Proclamation 11064 added motorboats of 8903.31 and 8903.32 and outboard motorboats of 8903.93.20 to the Section 338 list for Canada in U.S. note 51(b)(1) (9903.03.12), and Proclamation 11065 added outboard motorboats over 7.5 m (8903.99.21) to note 51(b)(3) (9903.03.14). The 50% applies even when USMCA is claimed.

changes.title: Section 338: 50% on Canadian floating docks, hulls, buoys and tanks
changes.detail: Proclamation 11048 (July 20, 2026) imposed a 50% duty on products of Canada in the list of U.S. note 51(b)(3) (9903.03.14), including floating docks (8905.90.10), other vessels and hulls (8906.90.00) and buoys, tanks and other floating structures (8907.90.00). Proclamation 11056 moved the start from August 19 to August 22, 2026. The duty applies even when USMCA is claimed.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 duties on 60 economies reach every Chapter 89 line
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duties on 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect. No Chapter 89 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or a country list (note 52(j)). For the EU and Taiwan the total is 10%, and for Japan and South Korea 12.5%, in place of lower base rates (note 52(k)). Canadian and Mexican goods entered under USMCA are exempt (notes 52(g)–(h)).

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil Section 301: 25% on every Chapter 89 line
changes.detail: The 25% duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. No Chapter 89 line is on its exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii), 9903.05.03).

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) on boats still apply.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. Canadian and Mexican goods entered under USMCA were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08); no Chapter 89 line was on its product exemption list.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025, and Proclamation 11030 implemented it in the HTS. AGOA (SPI D) makes every dutiable pleasure-boat line Free for eligible sub-Saharan countries; South Africa and Nigeria still pay the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), on every Chapter 89 line. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: Maritime Section 301 action suspended until November 9, 2026
changes.detail: Following the November 1, 2025 U.S.-China deal, USTR suspended every action in the investigation of China's targeting of the maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors from 12:01 a.m. EST on November 10, 2025 through 11:59 p.m. EST on November 9, 2026: the port fees on Chinese operators and owners and on Chinese-built ships, the fees on foreign-built vehicle carriers, and the 100% duties on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes (8426.19) and intermodal chassis (8716.39, 8716.90), whose Chapter 99 headings (9903.91.12–9903.91.16) now read "on or after November 10, 2026". None of these is a duty on Chapter 89 goods.

changes.title: China fentanyl-related IEEPA duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14357 cut the IEEPA duty on products of China from 20% to 10%. Chinese boats were also paying the 10% reciprocal duty and the Section 301 lists. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Maritime Section 301 modified: 100% on Chinese cranes and chassis
changes.detail: USTR changed the vehicle-carrier fee and imposed 100% duties on ship-to-shore cranes and on Chinese intermodal chassis and parts from November 9, 2025 (then suspended). No Chapter 89 line was included.

changes.title: USTR port fees on Chinese ships start (then suspended)
changes.detail: The first non-zero Section 301 service fees took effect: $50 per net ton for vessels with a Chinese operator or owner (Annex I) and, for other operators of Chinese-built vessels, the higher of $18 per net ton or $120 per container discharged (Annex II), charged up to five times a year per vessel and paid to CBP. They are fees on vessel calls, not import duties on the vessels or their cargo. Suspended from November 10, 2025.

changes.title: Country-specific reciprocal rates take effect
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country-specific reciprocal rates for many partners (for example 15% for the EU, all-inclusive). Chapter 89 boats and vessels paid them until February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil: 40% IEEPA duty
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added a 40% duty on products of Brazil (9903.01.77). No Chapter 89 line was on its exception list, so Brazilian boats and vessels paid it on top of the reciprocal tariff. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods, including boats, from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China IEEPA reciprocal rate cut to 10%
changes.detail: Chinese boats paid IEEPA duties on top of the Section 301 lists: a fentanyl-related 10% from February 4, 2025 (20% from March 4) and a reciprocal duty that rose to 125% in April 2025 and was cut to 10% from May 14, 2025. All ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USTR announces port fees on Chinese-operated and Chinese-built ships
changes.detail: USTR's action (effective April 17, 2025) set service fees charged per U.S. voyage on vessels with Chinese operators or owners and on Chinese-built vessels, rising each April through 2028, a fee on foreign-built vehicle carriers and a phased requirement to carry part of U.S. LNG exports on U.S.-built ships, and proposed duties on cranes and cargo-handling equipment. It placed no duty on the import of vessels.

changes.title: Executive Order 14269: Restoring America's Maritime Dominance
changes.detail: Directed a maritime action plan and told USTR to consider duties on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes and cargo-handling equipment in the Section 301 maritime investigation.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff covers boats and vessels
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico from April 5, 2025. No Chapter 89 line was on the Annex II exemption list. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Non-USMCA boats kept paying. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01), in force from March 4, 2025, including boats and vessels. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USTR finds China's maritime targeting actionable
changes.detail: USTR determined under Section 301 that China's targeting of the maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors for dominance is unreasonable and burdens U.S. commerce, opening the way for the 2025 port-fee action.

changes.title: China four-year review increases skip Chapter 89
changes.detail: USTR's four-year review raised Section 301 duties on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes, EVs, semiconductors, steel and other products (U.S. note 31). No Chapter 89 line is listed, so Chinese boats and vessels stayed at their List 1–4A rates.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 89 goods were **$3.06B in 2025**, down 19.4% from $3.80B in 2024 and well below the 2023 peak of $4.39B. **Pleasure boats (8903) were $2.51B, 82% of the total**: motorboats of 7.5–24 m alone (8903.32) were $782M, down from $1.27B, followed by small outboard boats, kayaks and canoes (8903.93, $609M) and motorboats over 24 m (8903.33, $467M).

The two largest suppliers are **Mexico** ($539M, 18%), almost all pleasure boats that enter Free under USMCA, and **Italy** ($527M, 17%), almost all yachts. **South Korea** jumped to third ($277M, from $3.3M) on one category: floating or submersible drilling and production platforms (8905.20, $277M in 2025 against $52K in 2024). Canada, France, the UK, China, Germany and Finland follow with $130M–$194M each, mostly boats; Türkiye's $117M is mainly 8905 vessels. Merchant ships (8901) are almost absent at $2.1M: ships in international trade are not entered for consumption, and foreign-built ships cannot serve U.S. domestic routes under the Jones Act.

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data, so the 2026 Section 301 duties (from July 2026) and the Canada Section 338 duties (from August 2026) are not yet visible in these figures. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duties for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule. Ships, tugs, platforms and floating structures are Free at base, so their totals are the extra duties alone; pleasure boats add a 1% to 2.7% base rate.

The country decides almost everything. **Mexican** boats that qualify for USMCA are Free. **EU** and **Taiwanese** goods pay exactly **10%** and **Japanese** and **Korean** goods **12.5%** (the 2026 Section 301 rate replaces lower base rates). The **UK**, **India** and other Section 301 economies add 10% or 12.5% to the base rate, and an FTA or AGOA claim (Australia, South Africa) removes only the base rate. **China** pays 25% (7.5% on warships and buoys) plus 12.5%; **Brazil** 25% plus 12.5%. **Canadian** motorboats, outboard boats, floating docks, hulls, buoys and tanks pay **50%** under Section 338 with or without USMCA; other Canadian boats are Free with USMCA. tariffEngineering.intro:
Importing a boat is mostly paperwork that agencies other than customs care about: a recreational boat needs a **Coast Guard hull identification number** and, if built for sale, the manufacturer's compliance label, and its gasoline engine must be **EPA-certified**. Ships face different rules: a **foreign-built ship can never get a coastwise endorsement**, so it cannot carry cargo or passengers between U.S. ports (the Jones Act), and a U.S.-flag ship that is repaired abroad owes a **50% duty on the foreign repair cost**, declared on CBP Form 226.

The legal ways to pay less: claim **USMCA** for Canadian and Mexican boats (it removes the 10% Section 301 duty but not Canada's 50% Section 338 duty), buy from a country outside the 60 Section 301 economies, classify by length and propulsion correctly, bring back a U.S.-built boat duty-free as **U.S. goods returned**, defer duty on a large yacht shown at a U.S. **boat show**, use the nonresident and racing provisions, and plan foreign shipyard work around the vessel repair exemptions. Each rule and lever links to its statute, regulation or HTS provision.

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican boats
levers.saves: The 1%–2.7% base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.29 / 9903.05.55)
levers.appliesTo: Boats and vessels of Canada or Mexico that meet the USMCA rule of origin
levers.document: USMCA certification of origin; SPI S on the entry
levers.caveat: Does not remove Canada's 50% Section 338 duty on motorboats, outboard boats, floating docks, hulls, buoys and tanks (note 51(a)). USMCA remains in force after the July 2026 joint review.

levers.title: Choose the country of build
levers.saves: Up to 30 points: 37.5%–40.2% from China or Brazil, 10% from the EU or Taiwan, 12.5% from Japan or Korea, the base rate alone from countries outside the 60 Section 301 economies
levers.document: Builder's certificate and commercial invoice showing where the hull was built and the vessel assembled
levers.caveat: Origin is where the vessel was built (substantially transformed), not where it was sold or last registered. FTA and AGOA claims remove only the base rate, not the Section 301 duty.

levers.title: Classify by type, length and propulsion
levers.saves: Between 1% (outboard motorboats), 1.5% (sailboats and inboard motorboats), 2.4% (inflatables), 2.7% (row boats) and Free (canoes, including kayaks); and between List 3 (25%) and List 4A (7.5%) for China
levers.document: Builder's specifications: length, hull material, engine type (outboard or inboard/outdrive), inflatable or rigid hull
levers.caveat: Chapter note 1 sends hulls and unfinished vessels without the character of a particular vessel to 8906. CBP classifies kayaks as canoes (Free), not as other row boats (2.7%). Ask CBP for a binding ruling when unsure.

citations.label: CBP ruling HQ H251131 (kayak classified as a canoe)

levers.title: Bring a U.S.-built boat back as U.S. goods returned
levers.saves: The whole duty, including the Section 301 and Section 338 duties
levers.appliesTo: U.S.-built boats and vessels returned without being improved abroad
levers.document: Proof of U.S. manufacture and export (HIN, builder's certificate, export record) for an entry under 9801.00.10
levers.caveat: Repairs or alterations made abroad are dutiable on their value under 9802.00.40 or 9802.00.50, and the 2026 Section 301 duty (note 52(a)) and Section 338 (note 51(a)) apply to that value.

levers.document: Importer certification and a bond of twice the duty for six months
levers.caveat: If sold within six months, entry is completed and duty paid at the value at import; if neither sold nor exported, duty is due when the bond period ends.

groups.note: Free. U.S.-documented fishing vessels owe the vessel repair duty on foreign repairs and nets (19 CFR 4.14(b)(1)).

groups.note: The only dutiable lines (1%–2.7%). Coast Guard HIN and safety standards and EPA engine certification apply; Canadian motorboats and outboard boats pay 50% Section 338.

groups.label: Tugs and pusher craft
groups.note: Free. A foreign-built tug cannot tow in U.S. coastwise trade (46 U.S.C. 55102).

groups.label: Dredgers, platforms, floating cranes and docks
groups.note: Free; floating docks 35% in column 2. Canadian floating docks pay 50% Section 338. Korea's platform hulls pay 12.5%.

groups.label: Warships, lifeboats and hulls
groups.note: Free. Hulls without the character of a particular vessel go here (chapter note 1). Canadian hulls and other vessels pay 50% Section 338; Chinese warships 20%.

groups.label: Rafts, buoys and floating structures
groups.note: Free; 45% in column 2. Canadian buoys, tanks and other floating structures pay 50% Section 338; Chinese buoys and tanks 20% (List 4A).

groups.label: Vessels for scrapping
groups.note: Free. Vessels imported for breaking up pay only the extra duties (China 37.5%).

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs on boats, yachts, ships and floating structures, by country, by HS code and for the maritime rules around them. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Base rates are low: ships, tugs, platforms and floating structures are Free, pleasure boats 1% to 2.7% (canoes Free). Pleasure boats were 82% of the $3.06B of 2025 imports.

The extra duties set the price: Free for USMCA boats from Mexico; 10% in total for the EU and Taiwan, 12.5% for Japan and Korea; base rate plus 10% or 12.5% for the UK and the other Section 301 economies; 37.5%–40.2% for China and Brazil; and 50% for Canadian motorboats, outboard boats, floating docks, hulls, buoys and tanks, even with USMCA.

The 2025 IEEPA duties ended February 24, 2026 and the Section 122 surcharge on July 23, 2026. USTR's port fees on Chinese ships are a vessel charge, not an import duty, and are suspended until November 9, 2026. U.S.-flag ships owe 50% on foreign repairs, and foreign-built vessels can never serve U.S. domestic routes (Jones Act).

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on imported boats?
faqs.answer: The general (MFN) rate on pleasure boats is 1% to 2.7% (8903; canoes and kayaks Free), and every ship, tug, platform and floating structure is Free. Most of the cost is the extra duties: USMCA boats from Mexico are Free; EU and Taiwanese boats pay 10% in total, Japanese and Korean 12.5%; UK pleasure boats 10% to 12.7%; boats from the other 2026 Section 301 economies the base rate plus 10% or 12.5%; Chinese and Brazilian boats 37.5% to 40.2%; Canadian motorboats and outboard boats 50%. Countries outside the 60 Section 301 economies pay only the base rate.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. import duty on yachts?
faqs.answer: A sailing yacht or motor yacht (8903.22, 8903.23, 8903.32, 8903.33) has a 1.5% base rate. From Italy, France, Germany, the Netherlands or another EU member the 2026 Section 301 duty makes the total exactly 10%; from Taiwan 10%; from Japan or South Korea 12.5%; from the UK 11.5%; from Türkiye 14%; from China 39%. A $1M Italian yacht pays $100,000. Yachts over 79 feet imported for sale at a U.S. boat show can defer the duty until sold (19 U.S.C. 1484b), and nonresidents cruising for pleasure pay no duty (additional U.S. note 1).

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on importing a boat from Canada to the U.S.?
searchedAs: importing a boat from canada to us
bringing a boat from canada to us
importing a used boat from canada to us
faqs.answer: It depends on the boat. Since September 15, 2026, Canadian motorboats of 8903.31 and 8903.32 and outboard motorboats of 8903.93.20 and 8903.99.21 pay a 50% Section 338 duty even with a USMCA claim, and 61% to 61.5% without one. Floating docks, hulls and buoys pay the same 50% since August 22, 2026. Other Canadian boats (sailboats, inflatables, canoes, kayaks) are Free with a USMCA claim and pay the base rate plus 10% Section 301 without it. A U.S.-built boat coming back from Canada unimproved is Free as U.S. goods returned (9801.00.10).

faqs.question: What duty do I pay when importing a boat from Europe to the U.S.?
searchedAs: importing a boat from europe to us
faqs.answer: For a boat built in an EU member state the total is 10% of the customs value on every Chapter 89 line (heading 9903.05.39 replaces the 1% to 2.7% base rate). UK-built boats pay the base rate plus 10% (10% to 12.7%) and Norwegian boats the base rate plus 12.5%. The 15% EU reciprocal rate of 2025 ended February 24, 2026. The boat also needs a Coast Guard hull identification number and an EPA-certified gasoline engine.

faqs.question: What is the import duty on boats from China?
searchedAs: import duty on boats from china
faqs.answer: Chinese pleasure boats pay the 1% to 2.7% base rate plus 25% under Section 301 List 3 (9903.88.03) and 12.5% under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.31): 38.5% for outboard boats, 39% for sailboats and inboard motorboats, 39.9% for inflatable boats, 40.2% for row boats, 37.5% for canoes and kayaks. Chinese ships, tugs and fishing vessels pay 37.5% (List 1), warships and buoys 20% (List 4A). No product exclusion covers Chapter 89. The IEEPA duties on China ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on used boats?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on used boats
import duty on second hand boats
faqs.answer: Yes. A used boat is classified and dutied like a new one, on its transaction value, by its country of build, so a used Italian yacht pays 10% and a used Chinese boat about 39%. The exception is a U.S.-built boat returned without improvement abroad, which is Free under 9801.00.10. Repairs done abroad on a U.S. boat are dutiable on their value (9802.00.50).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a boat?
faqs.answer: Boats and yachts are in heading 8903 of HTS Chapter 89: inflatable boats 8903.11–8903.19, sailboats 8903.21–8903.23 and motorboats other than outboard 8903.31–8903.33 (by length: up to 7.5 m, 7.5–24 m, over 24 m), and other boats 8903.93 (up to 7.5 m) and 8903.99: canoes and kayaks, row boats, outboard motorboats and others. Ships are 8901, fishing vessels 8902, tugs 8904, dredgers and platforms 8905, warships, lifeboats and hulls 8906, buoys and rafts 8907. The old 8903.10, 8903.91 and 8903.92 codes were replaced in 2022.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for an inflatable boat or RIB?
faqs.answer: Inflatable boats, including rigid hull inflatables (RIBs), are 8903.11 (fitted for a motor, up to 100 kg unladen), 8903.12 (not for a motor, up to 100 kg) or 8903.19 (other), all at 2.4%, Free under most FTAs. Boats over $500 are reported as with or without an attached rigid hull. Inflatable life rafts are 8907.10 (Free).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a kayak or canoe?
faqs.answer: Non-inflatable canoes and kayaks not designed principally for motors or sails are 8903.93.05 (up to 7.5 m) or 8903.99.06 (longer), Free: CBP ruled in HQ H251131 that a kayak is a canoe for this purpose. Other row boats of that kind (8903.93.15, 8903.99.16) pay 2.7%, and inflatable kayaks 2.4% (8903.11–8903.19). From China a kayak or canoe pays 37.5% (List 3 plus 12.5%); from the EU 10%.

faqs.question: Are boat parts, engines and trailers in Chapter 89?
faqs.answer: No. Chapter 89 covers whole vessels and hulls only. Outboard motors are 8407.21 (Free), other marine propulsion engines 8408.10 (diesel, 2.5%), propellers 8487.10 (Free) and trailers heading 8716; parts follow their own chapters. Each pays its own extra duties.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. port fees on Chinese ships?
searchedAs: us port fees on chinese ships
port fees on chinese built ships
ustr port fees on chinese ships
us suspends port fees on chinese ships
faqs.answer: Under its Section 301 action on China's maritime and shipbuilding sectors, USTR set fees per U.S. voyage: from October 14, 2025, $50 per net ton for ships with a Chinese operator or owner, and for other operators of Chinese-built ships the higher of $18 per net ton or $120 per container, rising each April to 2028, charged up to five times a year. They are charges on vessel calls collected by CBP, not import duties. USTR suspended them from November 10, 2025 through November 9, 2026.

faqs.question: Does Section 301 put a tariff on Chinese-built ships?
faqs.answer: Not on the maritime investigation. That action charges port fees on vessels and set 100% duties on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes and intermodal chassis (both suspended until November 9, 2026), not on ships. Chinese ships imported into the U.S. pay the 2018 China Section 301 duty instead: 25% for ships, fishing vessels and tugs (List 1), 7.5% for warships (List 4A), plus the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty.

faqs.question: What is the Jones Act and does it affect imported boats?
faqs.answer: Section 27 of the Merchant Marine Act of 1920 (46 U.S.C. 55102) lets only U.S.-built, U.S.-owned vessels with a coastwise endorsement carry merchandise between U.S. points; 46 U.S.C. 55103 does the same for passengers. Paying import duty does not change this: a foreign-built vessel cannot get a coastwise endorsement (46 U.S.C. 12112). Imported pleasure boats used privately are not affected.

faqs.question: What is CBP Form 226 and the 50% vessel repair duty?
faqs.answer: CBP Form 226 is the vessel repair declaration and entry. A vessel documented under U.S. law for foreign or coastwise trade owes duty of 50% of the foreign cost of equipment, parts and repairs on its first U.S. arrival (19 U.S.C. 1466; HTS 9818.00.07). Repairs in Canada, Mexico and Israel and in FTA partners listed in the special column are free, crew labor is excluded, and repairs forced by weather or casualty can be remitted (19 CFR 4.14).
